the_job.title: RL 1 — What a Branch Manager Is Actually For
the_job.desc: The job nobody defines. The five things only you can do, what you control against what you are measured on, the authority you under-use and the one you over-use, reading a branch from its floor, why doing the work yourself is the commonest first-management failure, and choosing what to fix first.

lessons.title: The job nobody defines
lessons.html:
Most branch managers are promoted from the floor, handed keys and a target, and left to work out the rest. It is the commonest career path in retail and it produces a predictable result: a person doing their old job harder, with more hours and more worry attached.

The distinction that changes everything, and it is not obvious from inside. A supervisor makes sure today goes well. A manager makes sure next quarter goes well, using today as evidence. Both matter, and only one of them is the job you were promoted into.

The trap is that the supervisory work is visible, urgent and satisfying. A queue you cleared, a delivery you sorted, a customer you calmed — you can see the result within the hour. Managerial work is slow, invisible and easy to postpone: the staff conversation you did not have, the stock line you did not analyse, the process you meant to fix. Nobody notices its absence for months, and then everybody notices at once.

What you were actually given. Not a bigger version of your old role. A small business to run, with a P&L, a stock position, a team, a customer base and a cash position. You did not choose the location, the range, the prices or most of the people — and you are still accountable for what the branch produces from them.

That gap between control and accountability is permanent, and it is worth accepting early rather than resenting for two years. Every branch manager in every chain has it. The skill is being precise about which side of the line a problem sits on, and this module is largely about learning to be precise about that.

The three questions that define the job.

What is this branch producing? Sales, margin, cash, stock health, customer return. Numbers you should know without asking.

What is it capable of producing? Given its location, size, range and team — because a branch performing well against its own potential is a different situation from one performing well against the estate.

What is stopping it? The honest answer, which is usually two or three specific things rather than a general shortage of effort.

Why the last one is where managers fail. Asked what is holding a branch back, most managers answer with something they cannot change — footfall, competition, head office pricing, the rent. Those may all be true and none of them is a plan. The useful answer is the biggest thing you could actually move, and finding it is the work.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Write down the three questions and answer them for your branch this week, in writing, without looking anything up. Then check your answers against the actual figures. The gap between what you believed and what is true is the most useful thing you will learn this month.

One reassurance, because this chapter can read as criticism. Nearly every branch manager in this market was promoted the same way and told the same nothing. If you recognise yourself in the supervisor description, that is not a failing on your part — it is the predictable result of a business that promoted its best floor person and assumed the rest would follow. The gap is in the preparation, not in you, and it closes quickly once somebody names it.

checks.why: Both matter, and only one of them is the job you were promoted into.

checks.why: Then everybody notices its absence at once.

lessons.title: The five things only you can do
lessons.html:
A branch manager's day fills itself. What separates managers who move a branch from managers who survive one is knowing which work genuinely requires them, and protecting time for it.

Five things nobody else in the branch can do.

1. Decide what matters this month. Everything cannot be a priority, and a team told everything matters will choose for themselves — usually whatever is most visible. Naming two or three things, out loud and repeatedly, is a manager's most under-used power.

2. Have the conversation nobody wants to have. The consistently late cashier. The storekeeper whose counts never balance. The supervisor who has stopped caring. These are yours alone, and every week you delay makes the conversation harder and the standard lower for everybody watching.

3. Look at the numbers and decide what they mean. Somebody else produces them. Only you can connect them to what you saw on the floor and conclude something.

4. Protect the standard. What you walk past, you accept. A shelf gap you do not mention, a till left unlocked, a rude exchange you did not address — each becomes the new normal within a fortnight, because the team is reading you constantly.

5. Represent the branch upward, honestly. Nobody at head office knows what your branch needs unless you say so, clearly, with evidence, at the time it can be acted on.

Everything else can, in principle, be done by somebody else. Serving, counting, receiving, cleaning, ordering — a manager doing these is either training somebody, covering an absence, or avoiding the five.

The avoidance is real and it is understandable. Serving customers is pleasant and you are good at it. The difficult conversation is unpleasant and you may not be. So the day fills with the pleasant work and the difficult item moves to tomorrow, week after week, and it is genuinely hard to see this happening from inside because you are working extremely hard throughout.

The test that catches it. At the end of a week, ask which of the five you did. If the honest answer is that you served, covered and firefighted, you had a busy week and not a managerial one. One such week is nothing. A quarter of them is why a branch drifts while its manager exhausts themselves.

WATCH-OUT: Being needed on the floor feels like being a good manager and is often the opposite. A branch that cannot run for two hours without you is not a compliment to your work — it is a description of something you have not yet built.

How to protect the time, practically. Not by working later. Block one hour, at the same point each week, when you are not on the floor and not available — and tell your team it exists and why, so that being unavailable is a known arrangement rather than you hiding in the office. Managers who try to find the time never find it; managers who take it out of the week in advance keep it about half the time, which is enough.

checks.why: Being needed on the floor feels like good management and is often the opposite.

lessons.title: What you are measured on, and what you actually control
lessons.html:
Most branch managers are measured on sales. Most branch managers control very little of what drives sales. Understanding that mismatch precisely is what lets you argue your case without sounding like you are making excuses.

Four levers you genuinely control.

Availability. Whether the thing a customer came for is on the shelf. Ordering discipline, receiving accuracy, replenishment from the back, and shrinkage — all branch-level, all yours.

Conversion and basket. How many people who walk in buy, and how much they buy. Service, layout, queue speed, staff knowledge, prompting.

Cost and loss. Rota against trade, overtime, utilities, waste, shrinkage. Small individually, material together, and almost entirely local.

The team. Who you hire, how they are trained, whether they stay. The slowest lever and the one that determines the other three.

Four things you do not control, and it is worth being unembarrassed about them: footfall, pricing, the range, and the location. Naming them accurately is not excuse-making — it is the precondition for a useful conversation with the people who do control them.

The distinction that makes you credible upward. "Sales are down because the market is difficult" is an excuse, whether or not it is true, because it invites no response. "Footfall is down 12% year on year, our conversion is up two points and basket is flat, so we are holding our share of a smaller market — and the two lines that lost us the most sales were out of stock for nine days each" is a report. Same situation, entirely different reception.

The second version requires you to know your numbers, which is module 2.

Where managers lose the argument. By claiming control they do not have — promising a sales recovery they cannot deliver — or by disclaiming control they do have, treating shrinkage or availability as somebody else's problem. Both damage credibility, and the second is the more common.

The habit worth building now. For any problem, say out loud which side of the line it sits on. Then act on the ones that are yours and report the ones that are not, with evidence, to somebody who can act. That is the whole of managing upward, and module 8 does the detail.

A caution about the four levers. They are not equally available to every branch. A small store with three staff cannot flex a rota the way a large one can; a branch with one supplier route has less to say about availability. Work out which of the four is most open to you at your branch specifically, because a manager pushing hard on the lever their situation has closed will exhaust themselves for very little.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: List your branch's five biggest problems and mark each as yours or not yours. Most managers find the split is roughly even — and that they have been spending their energy on the half they cannot move.

checks.q: 'Sales are down because the market is difficult' fails as a report because it:
checks.why: The same situation stated with footfall, conversion, basket and stockout days is a report rather than an excuse.

checks.q: Which lever is slowest and determines the other three?
checks.why: Who you hire, how they are trained, and whether they stay.

checks.q: The more common way managers lose credibility upward is by:
opts: Disclaiming control they have, such as shrinkage or availability
checks.why: Both damage credibility; treating a local problem as somebody else's is the frequent one.

lessons.title: Authority, and where it stops
lessons.html:
A branch manager has real authority over a small area and none at all over most of what affects them. Being clear about the boundary saves an extraordinary amount of wasted effort.

What you can usually decide alone. The rota. Who does what. How the floor is laid out within the standards you were given. Which local problems get attention first. How you spend your own time. Small discretionary spend. And every judgement about your own team's day-to-day performance.

What you can influence but not decide. Range and pricing. Headcount. Refurbishment. Systems and policy. Promotions. These need a case made to somebody else, which means evidence, timing and persistence rather than a request.

What is simply not yours. Group strategy, other branches, the terms of trade with suppliers, what the business chooses to invest in. Energy spent here is energy not spent on the first list.

The authority most managers under-use. Not budget or headcount — attention. What you look at, ask about and follow up on determines what your team treats as important, and you can redirect it entirely without permission from anybody.

A manager who asks about shrinkage every week gets a team that thinks about shrinkage. One who asks only about sales gets a team that thinks only about sales, whatever the wall poster says. That is a genuine lever, it costs nothing, and most managers never think of it as authority at all.

The authority most managers over-use. Deciding things their team could decide. Every decision you take that somebody else could have taken trains them to bring you the next one, and within a year you are the bottleneck for a branch of thirty people and cannot understand why you have no time.

Where the boundary is genuinely unclear, ask once and in writing. Many branch managers operate for years unsure whether they may authorise something, and resolve it by either never doing it or quietly doing it and hoping. Both are worse than a two-line email that settles it permanently.

And the authority you inherit without being told. Whatever your predecessor did, your team assumes you will do — the exceptions they were allowed, the standards that had slipped, the things nobody checked. You are not bound by any of it, but you will have to actively change what you want changed, and the first month is when that is cheapest. Change it later and it reads as a new rule; change it early and it is simply how you run the branch.

WATCH-OUT: A manager who says yes to every decision brought to them is not being helpful. They are teaching a team not to think, and the cost arrives later as a branch that cannot function in their absence — including on the day they are promoted.

checks.q: You want your team to take shrinkage seriously but have no budget and no new headcount. The lever available is:
opts: Asking about it every week, because what you ask about is what they think about
checks.why: It costs nothing, needs nobody's permission, and most managers never treat it as authority at all.

lessons.title: Reading a branch from the floor
lessons.html:
Before the numbers arrive, a branch tells you how it is doing. Learning to read it is a genuine skill and it is faster than any report — a manager who walks their floor properly knows most of what next week's figures will say.

What to look at, in the order it matters.

Gaps. Empty facings on lines that should be there. A gap is a sale you did not make and a customer who may not come back for it. Count them on the lines that matter rather than everywhere.

The queue. Not just its length — whether it is moving, whether anybody is doing anything about it, and whether people are leaving it. A customer who abandons a queue is invisible in every report you will ever read.

Where your staff's eyes are. On customers, on each other, or on their phones. This tells you more about your team's condition than any conversation, and it is visible in ten seconds.

Cleanliness and order in the parts customers do not see. The stockroom, the back office, the yard. Front-of-house standards are performed for visitors; the back is what standards actually are.

What customers do rather than what they buy. Where they pause, what they pick up and put down, what they ask for and do not find, where they look lost. Twenty minutes standing still and watching is worth more than an hour of walking about.

The two walks worth doing deliberately. One at your busiest hour, because that is when everything strains and the weaknesses show. One at your quietest, because that is when standards slip and habits form. Managers who only walk mid-morning see a branch that exists at no other time of day.

And the walk you have stopped doing. After a year in a branch you stop seeing it. The gap has been there so long it is furniture; the sign has been crooked since you arrived. The fix is to walk it with somebody else — a manager from another branch, a new starter in their first week — and ask what they notice. New eyes find in ten minutes what familiar ones have stopped registering.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Once a month, walk your branch with a colleague from another store and swap. Ask only one question of each other: what would you change first? It costs two hours, it is free, and it is the single most effective way to see your own branch again.

What to do with what the walk tells you. Write it down at the time, on the floor, rather than trusting that you will remember at your desk. Three or four specific things beats a general impression, and the specific ones can be assigned to somebody with a date attached. A walk that produces a feeling that the branch is a bit untidy changes nothing; one that produces four named items changes four things.

checks.q: Six people leave your queue on a Saturday afternoon. Next week's figures will show:
opts: Nothing at all — an abandoned queue is invisible in every report
A conversion dip you can trace
checks.why: Which is why whether the queue is moving matters more than how long it is.

checks.q: Your shop floor is immaculate and the stockroom is chaotic. What this tells you is:
opts: Front-of-house is being performed, and the back is your real standard
checks.why: The parts customers never see are the honest measure of what a branch actually keeps to.

checks.q: After a year in a branch you stop seeing it. The remedy is to:
opts: Walk it with somebody else and ask what they notice
checks.why: New eyes find in ten minutes what familiar ones have stopped registering.

lessons.title: The trap of doing the work
lessons.html:
The most common failure in a first management role is not laziness or incompetence. It is a capable person doing too much themselves, for entirely good reasons, until the branch depends on it.

Why it happens, and none of the reasons is stupid. You are faster. The standard matters and you are not sure they will meet it. Explaining takes longer than doing. The customer is waiting now. And, underneath, doing the work is comfortable and managing is not.

What it costs, in the order the costs arrive.

Your time first, which was the resource that made you useful.

Then their development, because somebody who is never allowed to do a thing badly never learns to do it well.

Then their motivation, since being trusted with nothing is not a pleasant way to work, and the good ones leave first.

Then the branch's resilience, because a store that works only when you are in it fails the week you are ill — and every week you are not there, which is more weeks than you think.

The delegation that actually works. Not handing over tasks — handing over outcomes, with the standard stated and the method left alone. "Make sure the chilled section is full and rotated by nine every morning, and tell me if you cannot" is an outcome. "Fill the chilled section" is a task you will be checking forever.

And accepting the first attempts will be worse. This is the part people cannot get past. The first three times somebody else does it, it will be slower and rougher than your version, and you will be tempted to take it back. Taking it back teaches them they were right to doubt themselves and teaches you that delegation does not work. The fourth attempt is usually fine.

What to keep. Not everything delegates. Discipline, pay conversations, anything involving a person's standing, and the final call on money — these are yours and handing them down is not delegation but abdication. The rule is simple enough: delegate the work, never the accountability.

WATCH-OUT: The phrase to be suspicious of in your own head is "it is quicker if I just do it." It is quicker today, every time, and that is precisely why it is a trap — the cost is never visible on the day you pay it.

Where to start, if this is your pattern. Not with the most important thing you do. Pick something routine, visible and low-risk — the opening checks, the weekly order for one category, the rota draft — hand it over properly with the standard stated, and leave it alone for a month. The point of starting small is not caution about the task; it is that you need to prove to yourself that the branch survives, and one successful handover makes the next three far easier.

checks.q: You catch yourself thinking 'it is quicker if I just do it'. The reason that thought is dangerous is:
opts: It is correct today, every time, and the cost never shows on the day you pay it
checks.why: The costs arrive later, in order: your time, their development, their motivation, the branch's resilience.

checks.q: Delegation that works hands over:
opts: Outcomes, with the standard stated and the method left alone
checks.why: 'Full and rotated by nine, tell me if you cannot' is an outcome; 'fill the section' is a task you check forever.

checks.q: Your best supervisor offers to handle a lateness conversation for you. You should:
opts: Decline: anything affecting a person's standing stays with you
checks.why: Delegate the work, never the accountability.

lessons.title: Deciding what to do first
lessons.html:
A branch produces more problems than any manager can address. Most managers respond by working longer. The alternative is choosing deliberately, and choosing well is most of what separates branches that improve from branches that merely cope.

The two questions that rank almost anything. How much is this costing? and can I actually move it? High cost and movable goes first. Low cost or immovable can wait however loudly it is complaining.

That sounds obvious and it is routinely violated, because attention follows noise rather than value. The loudest problem in a branch is rarely the most expensive one.

Put a number on it, even a rough one. A line out of stock nine days a month, selling four a day at ₦1,200 with 30% margin, is costing about ₦13,000 of margin monthly at that branch. The customer complaint that took an hour of your week last month cost considerably less. Both feel urgent; only one is worth your quarter.

The arithmetic does not need to be precise. It needs to exist, because a rough number beats a strong feeling every time.

The three-thing rule. Name three priorities for the month, write them where your team can see them, and repeat them until people are tired of hearing them. Not ten. Three is roughly what a team can hold, and a manager with ten priorities has none — the team simply picks whichever they prefer.

Distinguish fixing from firefighting. Firefighting is dealing with the instance: the gap filled, the complaint settled, the shift covered. Fixing is dealing with the cause: why the gap keeps appearing, why that complaint recurs, why the rota keeps failing. Firefighting is unavoidable and it is not progress, and a manager who only firefights will do the same fire every month for a year.

The hour that pays for itself. One hour a week, protected, spent on a cause rather than an instance. Not more — one hour, genuinely uninterrupted, on the biggest thing on your list. Over a quarter that is thirteen hours on causes, which is more than most branch managers spend in a year, and it is where the difference actually comes from.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Write your three priorities on paper and keep them visible on your desk. When something new arrives, ask whether it is bigger than one of the three. If it is not, it waits — and if it is, something comes off the list rather than being added to it.

Tell your manager what the three are. Two things follow from doing it. Head office stops assuming you are working on whatever they last mentioned, and you gain a reason to decline the fourth thing that arrives — not a refusal, but a question about which of the three should come off. A manager with visible priorities is much harder to load arbitrarily than one whose list nobody has seen.

checks.q: A line out of stock nine days a month costs ₦13,000 of margin; a complaint cost an hour last month. You should work on:
opts: The stockout, because a rough number beats a strong feeling
checks.why: Attention follows noise rather than value, and the loudest problem is rarely the most expensive.

checks.q: A manager with ten priorities has:
opts: None — the team picks whichever they prefer
checks.why: Three is roughly what a team can hold, and a longer list simply hands the choice back to them.

checks.q: Firefighting deals with the instance; fixing deals with the cause. A manager who only firefights will:
opts: Do the same fire every month for a year
checks.why: One protected hour a week on a cause is thirteen hours a quarter, and it is where the difference comes from.

lessons.title: Okelewo Stores, three years on
lessons.html:
The retailer from the counter track has grown. Three branches became eleven across Ogun and Lagos, staff went from thirty to a hundred and forty, and the founder no longer knows every person by name. What worked at three branches has stopped working, and the reason is worth understanding because it is the standard path.

What changed, and it is not what people expect. The systems held. Prices are central, counters are governed by profiles, shifts are counted, and the figures are trustworthy. The thing that broke was management: eleven branches need eleven people making local decisions well, and the business had promoted eleven good supervisors and given them keys.

Three managers, and the pattern in each is common enough to be worth naming.

Lalubu, the flagship. The manager is the best cashier the business ever had and still serves at the busiest hour every day. Customers love her. Her branch has the highest sales in the group and the third-worst shrinkage, because the storeroom runs itself and nobody has looked at it in a year. She works fifty-five hours and cannot say why she is tired.

Sango, the second Abeokuta shop. The manager delegates well and reads his figures. His branch is unremarkable on every measure and has the lowest staff turnover in the group. Head office regards him as steady rather than strong — and he is quietly the most valuable manager in the business, because his branch runs without him and he develops people other branches later take.

Ikeja. The manager is ambitious, chases the sales target, and has run three promotions this quarter without asking what they cost. Sales are up nine per cent and margin is down two points, which on that branch's volume is a loss. He does not know this, because he reads the sales report and not the margin one.

What the founder eventually noticed. Not that any of the three was bad. That all three were doing what they had been rewarded for — serving, steadying and selling — and that nobody had ever told them the job was something else. The eleven managers had eleven private definitions of the role, and the business had never written one down.

The uncomfortable conclusion for a growing retailer. Promoting your best floor staff is the right instinct and an incomplete plan. The skills that make somebody excellent on the floor — speed, presence, willingness to do it themselves — are precisely the ones that make a mediocre manager if nothing is added to them.

What Okelewo did about it. Not a restructure. They wrote down what a branch manager is for — roughly the five things in chapter two — and they changed what they asked about in the monthly call, which had been sales and became sales, margin, shrinkage, availability and staff turnover. Within two quarters the Ikeja manager was reading his margin report, because it had become something he was asked about. That is the attention lever from chapter four, applied from above.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Ask yourself which of the three you most resemble. Most managers recognise themselves in one within a sentence or two, and the recognition is more useful than any amount of general advice about leadership.

checks.q: The Lalubu manager has the highest sales and third-worst shrinkage. The cause is:
opts: She serves at the busiest hour and nobody has looked at the storeroom in a year
checks.why: She is doing what she was rewarded for, at fifty-five hours a week.

checks.q: The Ikeja manager's sales are up nine per cent and margin down two points. He does not know because:
opts: He reads the sales report and not the margin one
checks.why: On that branch's volume it is a loss, and it is invisible from the report he reads.

checks.q: What broke as Okelewo grew from three branches to eleven was:
opts: Management — eleven people now make local decisions
checks.why: The systems held; the business had promoted eleven good supervisors and given them keys.

lessons.title: Review, and what this track covers
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the assessment, then read what follows.

The job (Chapter 1). A supervisor makes today go well; a manager makes next quarter go well using today as evidence. Three questions: what is this branch producing, what is it capable of, what is stopping it — and the third is answered with something you can move.

The five (Chapter 2). Decide what matters, have the hard conversation, read the numbers and conclude something, protect the standard, represent the branch upward. Everything else can be done by somebody else. A busy week is not automatically a managerial one.

Control and accountability (Chapter 3). You control availability, conversion and basket, cost and loss, and the team. You do not control footfall, pricing, range or location. Name which side a problem sits on, act on yours, report the rest with evidence.

Authority (Chapter 4). Under-used: attention. Over-used: deciding what your team could decide. Where the boundary is unclear, ask once in writing.

The floor (Chapter 5). Gaps, the queue moving, where your staff's eyes are, the parts customers do not see, and what customers do rather than buy. Walk at your busiest and quietest hours, and once a month with somebody else's eyes.

Delegation (Chapter 6). Hand over outcomes with the standard stated. Accept the first three attempts will be worse. Delegate the work, never the accountability.

Priorities (Chapter 7). How much is it costing, and can I move it. Three priorities, visible and repeated. One protected hour a week on a cause rather than an instance.

Okelewo (Chapter 8). The systems held and management did not. Three managers, each doing what they were rewarded for, none told the job was something else.

What comes next. Reading your branch's numbers and knowing which ones lie. Availability and the shelf. People — hiring, training, the difficult conversation, and why they leave. Loss, and what a manager does about it that an auditor cannot. Customers and your local market. Managing upward. And the manager's operating week, which pulls all of it into a rhythm you can actually keep.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Before moving on, do the chapter one exercise if you have not: answer the three questions in writing, then check against the figures. Everything in the modules that follow assumes you know your own branch's numbers, and most managers discover they knew them less well than they thought.

How to use this track if you are already in the job. Do not wait until the end to change anything. Each module has one practice worth starting the week you read it — the three questions here, the numbers in module 2, the availability check in module 3. A manager who finishes the track having changed nothing has read a book; one who starts a single habit per module arrives at the end running a different branch.

questions.why: Act on yours; report the rest with evidence to somebody who can act.

questions.q: The authority most branch managers under-use is:
questions.why: What you ask about weekly is what your team thinks about.

opts: Thinks only about sales, whatever the poster says
questions.why: It costs nothing to redirect and most managers never treat it as authority.

questions.q: Taking a decision your team could take teaches them to:
questions.why: Within a year you are the bottleneck for a branch of thirty.

questions.q: Where your authority is unclear you should:
questions.why: Never doing it and quietly doing it are both worse.

questions.q: Which is NOT something a branch manager can usually decide alone?
questions.why: Headcount is influenced by making a case, not decided.

questions.q: A customer who abandons your queue appears:

questions.q: The two deliberate walks are at your busiest hour and:
questions.why: Busy shows the strain; quiet is when standards slip and habits form.

opts: Walking it with somebody else's eyes
questions.why: New eyes find in ten minutes what familiar ones no longer register.

questions.q: Twenty minutes standing still and watching customers is worth more than:
questions.why: Where they pause, what they put down, what they ask for and do not find.

questions.q: 'It is quicker if I just do it' is a trap because:
opts: It is true today every time, and the cost is invisible on the day

opts: Your time, their development, their motivation, the branch's resilience

questions.why: 'Full and rotated by nine, tell me if you cannot' is an outcome.

questions.q: Which must not be delegated?
questions.why: Delegate the work, never the accountability.

questions.q: The two questions that rank almost any problem are how much it costs and:
questions.why: High cost and movable goes first.

questions.q: Attention in a branch tends to follow:
questions.why: The loudest problem is rarely the most expensive one.

questions.q: A rough cost estimate is worth having because:
opts: A rough number beats a strong feeling

questions.q: How many priorities should a manager name for the month?

questions.q: A manager who only firefights will:
opts: Do the same fire every month for a year

questions.why: More than most branch managers spend on causes in a year.

questions.q: At Okelewo, growth from three branches to eleven broke:
questions.why: The systems held; eleven good supervisors had been given keys.

questions.why: Doing what she was rewarded for, at fifty-five hours a week.

opts: He reads sales and not margin
questions.why: On that branch's volume, nine per cent more sales at two points less margin is a loss.

opts: Doing what they had been rewarded for, never told the job was something else

questions.q: Promoting your best floor staff is:

the_numbers.title: RL 2 — Reading Your Branch's Numbers
the_numbers.desc: Which figures on a branch report are true, which are artefacts of how the group allocates, and what to look at each week. Sales broken into its four parts, margin and why yours moved, availability as a number, shrinkage read honestly, controllable against allocated cost, the numbers that lie, and a weekly routine of six figures.

lessons.title: The reports you get, and the ones you need
lessons.html:
Most branch managers receive a sales report daily, a P&L monthly, and a stock report when somebody asks for one. That is what the business happens to produce, and it is not the same thing as what the job requires.

What you are usually given. Sales against target, by day and month. Sometimes footfall or transaction count. A monthly branch P&L with costs allocated down from the centre. A stock valuation figure.

What that set is missing, and each gap matters.

Margin, not just sales. A branch can grow sales and lose money, and the sales report will never say so. The Ikeja manager from module 1 is the standard case.

Availability. Sales tell you what you sold. Nothing on a standard report tells you what a customer came for and did not find, which is the largest recoverable loss in most branches.

Shrinkage, at branch and category level. Frequently buried inside cost of sales as a residual and never isolated, so nobody can say what it actually is.

Which costs are yours. A branch P&L usually mixes costs you control with costs allocated from the centre, and presents them as one number you are held to.

The two questions to ask about any report before you read it. Who produced it, and from what? A figure assembled from the system is different evidence from one somebody typed into a spreadsheet, and a manager who does not know which they are holding will defend a number they cannot support.

Asking for what you need. Most managers assume the reporting is fixed. Usually it is not — the data exists and nobody asked for it in that shape. A specific request, made once, with a reason attached, succeeds far more often than managers expect: not "can I have better reports" but "can I have margin by category monthly, because I cannot tell whether promotions are helping or hurting."

And the honest position if the answer is no. Build the two or three numbers yourself, roughly, from what you can see. A rough margin figure you produced beats an accurate one you do not have — and a manager who has been tracking something by hand for three months has a much stronger case for it being reported properly.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: List the numbers you receive and the ones you would need to answer the three questions from module 1. The gap is usually two or three figures, and asking for them specifically, once, with a reason, is a ten-minute job most managers never do.

One more thing to establish about any report: when it arrives. A monthly pack landing on the twenty-fifth describes a period that ended nearly two months earlier, by which time every decision it might have informed has been taken. If yours is late, ask for it a week earlier and accept it will be slightly less accurate. Almost every business can do this, almost none has been asked, and the week of relevance is worth more than the accuracy given up.

checks.q: Sales grew nine per cent at your branch and you are told it was a good month. Before agreeing you need:
opts: Margin, because a branch can grow sales and lose money
checks.why: The sales report will never tell you that, which is the Ikeja case from module 1.

checks.q: The largest recoverable loss in most branches appears on:
opts: No standard report at all — what a customer came for and did not find
checks.why: Sales tell you what you sold, not what you failed to sell.

checks.q: Asking for a report you do not get succeeds far more often when phrased as:
opts: A specific figure with the reason you need it
checks.why: The data usually exists and nobody asked for it in that shape.

lessons.title: Sales: the number everybody watches
lessons.html:
Sales is the figure your branch is judged on, discussed in every meeting, and the one that tells you least about whether the month was any good.

Break it into its parts, because only the parts are actionable. Sales equals transactions multiplied by average basket. Transactions come from footfall multiplied by conversion. So four numbers sit under the one, and a change in sales is always a change in at least one of them.

Why this matters more than it sounds. "Sales are down eight per cent" gives you nothing to do. "Footfall is down twelve, conversion is up two points and basket is flat" tells you the market shrank and your team held its share — which is a completely different conversation and a completely different action.

What each part tells you.

Footfall is mostly not yours. Weather, the market, a competitor opening, roadworks, the estate that feeds you. Worth knowing precisely so you can say what happened without sounding defensive.

Conversion is yours. Service, availability, queue speed, layout. A conversion drop with footfall steady is a branch problem, and it is the single most useful signal on this list.

Basket is partly yours. Range and pricing are not, but prompting, adjacency, availability of the second item and staff knowledge are.

If you do not measure footfall, and many branches do not, transactions are the usable substitute. Transaction count against last year, at the same point in the week, tells you most of what footfall would.

The comparison that misleads and the one that does not. Comparing to last month compares different weather, different promotions and a different number of paydays. Compare like periods — this week against the same week last year, this Saturday against Saturdays. Month-on-month movement in a seasonal business tells you about the calendar rather than about your branch.

And treat the target as what it is. A target is somebody's expectation set before the year began. Missing it can mean the branch underperformed, or that the expectation was wrong. Both happen, and a manager who can distinguish them with the four numbers is worth listening to; one who only knows they missed is not.

A note on daily sales figures. They are the most-watched and least informative numbers in retail. A single day contains weather, one large basket, a delivery that did not arrive, and a public holiday nobody remembered — none of which says anything about the branch. Read them for exceptions rather than for trend, and hold judgement until the week is complete. Managers who react daily teach their teams that the number moves for reasons nobody can influence, which is precisely the wrong lesson.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Every week, write down four numbers rather than one: transactions, basket, and the two compared with the same week last year. It takes five minutes and it converts every sales conversation you will have that month from an argument into a diagnosis.

checks.q: Sales are down eight per cent. Footfall is down twelve, conversion up two points, basket flat. This means:
opts: The market shrank and your team held its share
checks.why: The same fall, read four ways instead of one, produces a different conversation entirely.

checks.q: Which part of the sales equation is most usefully treated as a branch problem?
checks.why: A conversion drop with footfall steady is the single most useful signal available.

checks.q: Comparing this month to last month in a seasonal business tells you about:
checks.why: Compare like periods — this week against the same week last year, Saturdays against Saturdays.

lessons.title: Margin, and why yours moved
lessons.html:
Gross margin is what is left of each naira of sales after the goods themselves are paid for. Sell ₦100 of goods that cost you ₦70 and your gross margin is ₦30, or 30%. It is not the same as markup, which is the uplift on cost — the same transaction is a 30% margin and a 43% markup, and confusing the two is how a branch prices for 40% and achieves 29%.

Four things move it, and this chapter is about which of the four you can see at branch level, which you caused, and what to do in the week you notice.

The four movers, in the order a branch manager can act on them.

Mix — what sold, not what it sold for. The commonest cause and the one most often missed, because every individual product margin looks correct. A month heavy in low-margin categories drops blended margin with nothing wrong anywhere.

Discount and markdown — what you gave away, deliberately or otherwise. Yours, visible, and reportable by reason if the counter is configured as the ZhiftPOS track describes.

Loss — shrinkage arriving as a lower margin with no label attached, which the next chapter covers.

Buying price — rarely yours, and worth checking rather than assuming, because a supplier increase can pass through without anybody telling the branches.

The order to check them in. Mix first, because it is the most likely and the easiest to see. Then markdown, which is reportable. Then loss. Buying price last, because you can rarely do anything about it and it is the one most managers reach for first.

What a two-point move is worth. On a branch turning over ₦18,000,000 a month, two points of margin is ₦360,000 monthly — roughly ₦4.3m a year. That is usually larger than every cost saving a branch manager is asked to find, and it moves without anybody deciding anything.

Which is why margin deserves the attention sales gets. A manager who reads only sales can lose ₦4.3m a year without a single bad day appearing in any report they read. That is not a hypothetical: it is precisely the Ikeja situation from module 1, and it lasted three quarters.

What to do in the week you notice. Do not announce a margin problem. Decompose it first — pull the category split and compare with the prior period, look at markdown by reason, check whether any large line's cost moved. You will usually find one or two categories carrying the whole movement, and a specific finding gets acted on where a general concern gets nodded at.

Where a branch manager most often causes a margin fall without noticing. Not through discounting, which is visible, but through what gets promoted, displayed and pushed. Front-of-store space given to a low-margin category, staff prompting the cheaper alternative because it is easier to sell, a display built where a supplier funded it — each shifts mix without any decision that looks like a pricing decision. Which makes mix worth more attention than it usually gets: it is the only margin lever that improves without asking a single customer to pay more.

WATCH-OUT: A margin fall with sales up is the pattern to fear most, because everything on the surface looks like success and the branch will be congratulated while it earns less. Check margin whenever sales rise sharply, not only when they fall.

checks.q: Margin fell and sales rose. This pattern is dangerous because:
opts: Everything on the surface looks like success while the branch earns less
checks.why: Check margin whenever sales rise sharply, not only when they fall.

checks.q: The first of the four movers to check is:
checks.why: It is the most likely cause and the easiest to see, and every individual product margin still looks correct.

checks.q: Two points of margin on a branch turning over ₦18m a month is worth about:
checks.why: Roughly ₦4.3m a year, usually larger than every cost saving a branch manager is asked to find.

lessons.title: Availability, as a number
lessons.html:
The largest recoverable loss in most branches is invisible on every report, because a sale that did not happen leaves no record. Turning availability into a number is the single highest-value measurement a branch manager can introduce.

Why it matters more than it appears. A customer who cannot find one item frequently leaves without the other four they came for, and some of them do not come back for a month. The loss is not the one line — it is the basket and a portion of the relationship.

Rank by contribution rather than by sales, and the distinction matters. Contribution is what a line leaves you after the cost of the goods themselves — its selling price less what you paid for it. A line selling ₦900,000 a month at 8% leaves you ₦72,000; one selling ₦300,000 at 35% leaves ₦105,000. The second is smaller on every sales report and worth more to your branch, and an availability check built on sales value will watch the wrong forty lines.

How to measure it without a system that does it for you. Take your top forty lines by contribution, walk them at the same time twice a week, and count how many are unavailable. That is your availability rate on the lines that matter, it takes fifteen minutes, and almost no branch has the figure.

Where the system helps. Where stock is tracked, a report of lines at zero on hand tells you what is out now. What it will not tell you is how long it was out or how often, which is why the manual count twice a week is worth keeping — a line out for six hours on a Tuesday is not the same problem as one out every weekend.

Converting it to money, which is what makes anybody act. A line selling four a day at ₦1,200 with 30% margin, out for nine days in the month, cost roughly ₦13,000 of margin at that branch. Multiply across the lines that are habitually out and the number is usually startling — and it is the number that gets a replenishment problem taken seriously where a complaint about gaps does not.

The four causes, and they need different fixes. Not ordered — an ordering discipline problem. Ordered and not delivered — a supplier or central problem, which is reportable rather than yours. Delivered and not on the shelf — a replenishment problem, and the most common of the four. Or on the shelf and unfindable, which is a layout problem and is invisible to every count you will do.

That third cause deserves emphasis because it is both the most frequent and the most fixable. Stock sitting in the back while the shelf is empty is a branch losing sales on goods it already paid for, and no system report will identify it — only somebody walking the floor with the stock figure in their hand.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Count your top forty lines twice a week for a month and price the gaps. That single exercise produces the most persuasive number a branch manager can put in front of head office, because it is a loss the business is already suffering and had never quantified.

What to do with the count once you have it. Do not send it upward immediately. Fix the third cause first — stock in the back that is not on the shelf — because it is yours, it is usually the largest, and it takes a replenishment routine rather than a request to anybody. Then report what remains, which will be the ordering and supply causes, with the money attached. A manager who has already fixed their own half is heard very differently from one reporting the whole problem outward.

checks.q: A customer cannot find one item on their list. The realistic loss is:
opts: The basket, and a portion of the relationship
Nothing if they buy the rest
checks.why: Some of them do not come back for a month.

checks.q: Which cause of unavailability is most frequent and most fixable?
opts: Delivered but not on the shelf
checks.why: Stock in the back while the shelf is empty is a branch losing sales on goods it already paid for.

checks.q: Availability should be measured on your top lines by:
checks.why: Following the finance track's argument — the biggest sellers are not always where the money is.

lessons.title: Shrinkage, read honestly
lessons.html:
The internal control track teaches an auditor to test for loss. This chapter is the manager's side of the same problem: what your shrinkage number means, what it is made of, and what you can actually do about it before anybody audits anything.

What it is made of, and the order surprises people. Administrative error is usually the largest component — miscounts, mis-scans, wrong units, cut-off mistakes. Then supplier shortfall: invoiced and not delivered, or delivered short and signed for. Then internal theft. Then customer theft, which most managers assume dominates and rarely does. Then damage and expiry.

Why the order matters to you specifically. A manager who treats all shrinkage as theft spends their attention on the smallest component and on the part of it involving their own staff, which is corrosive and usually wrong. The first two components are process problems, they are yours, and they are fixable without accusing anybody.

Getting a number at all. Many businesses never isolate shrinkage — it emerges as a residual inside cost of sales, blended with mix and pricing, and nobody can say what it was. If that is your situation, producing a defensible shrinkage figure by category is itself a substantial piece of work and probably the most valuable thing you will do this year.

Read it as a percentage and by category. Naira ranks by branch size and tells you nothing. As a percentage of sales, compared within category, you can see whether your loss is concentrated or spread. Concentrated points at a specific process, location or person; spread points at counting, receiving or systemic error.

The receiving bay is where a manager has most leverage. It is the point where the business's money becomes its goods, it is usually staffed by the most junior person available, under time pressure with a driver waiting — and a receipt that always exactly matches the order is not a good sign. Real deliveries are occasionally short. A receiver whose figures never differ is copying rather than counting.

And the count nobody trusts. If your counts are done by whoever is responsible for the stock, you do not have a count — you have a confirmation. Rotating who counts what, at no cost, changes the quality of the number more than any amount of exhortation about accuracy.

And what a manager can do that an auditor cannot. An auditor tests and reports; you are there every day. The things that actually reduce shrinkage are unglamorous and local — a receiving bay where somebody counts, a back door that is not propped open, a rota that does not leave one person alone with the stockroom, waste recorded when it happens rather than reconstructed at month end. None of that appears in an audit finding, and all of it moves the number.

WATCH-OUT: Be suspicious of your own good news. A branch whose count differences are always small and always favourable is more often a branch where the count is being adjusted to agree with the system than one where nothing is going missing.

checks.q: Your shrinkage figure is unchanged and small every month. This is:
opts: More often a count adjusted to agree with the system than a branch losing nothing
checks.why: Genuine counting produces differences in both directions and of varying size.

checks.q: A manager treating all shrinkage as theft will:
opts: Spend attention on the smallest component, and on their own staff
checks.why: Administrative error and supplier shortfall are larger, are process problems, and are fixable without accusing anybody.

checks.q: A receiver whose quantities always exactly match the order is:
checks.why: Real deliveries are occasionally short, damaged or over.

lessons.title: Costs: yours, and the other kind
lessons.html:
A branch P&L usually mixes costs you decide with costs allocated to you from the centre, presents them as one figure, and holds you to the total. Separating the two is the difference between a cost conversation that goes somewhere and one that goes in circles.

Costs that are genuinely yours. The rota and overtime, which is usually the largest controllable cost in a branch. Utilities, to the extent behaviour affects them. Consumables. Waste and damage. Local repairs and small discretionary spend. Cash losses.

Costs allocated to you. A share of head office, group insurance, systems, marketing, sometimes distribution. These arrive by a rule somebody chose, often years ago, and they change when the rule changes rather than when anything happens at your branch.

The point branch managers most need to be able to make. An allocated cost does not disappear if the activity does. A branch showing a loss after allocation may be contributing substantially toward group overhead, and closing it would make the group worse off — the overhead simply redistributes onto the branches that remain.

So the number to know about your own branch is its contribution: sales, less cost of sales, less the costs that would genuinely stop if the branch stopped. That is the figure that says whether your branch earns its keep, and it is frequently a great deal healthier than the bottom line you are shown.

Where the rota deserves its own attention. It is the one large cost a manager adjusts weekly, and most rotas are built from availability and habit rather than from trade. Compare your staffing profile to your hourly sales profile for one week: most branches find they are overstaffed in the morning and short at the times that actually convert. Fixing that costs nothing and improves both the cost line and the conversion line at once.

And a caution about cutting. Cost reduction at branch level is real and it is small. Two points of margin, or a fixed availability problem, is usually worth more than every controllable cost saving available — which is why the previous chapters come first in this module rather than last.

The cost conversation worth having upward. When head office asks for a percentage off branch costs, the useful reply is not a refusal or a promise. It is what that percentage represents at your branch, what it would come out of, and what it would cost elsewhere — hours removed from the trading hours that convert, for instance. Costs are real and so are the consequences of cutting the wrong ones, and a manager who can show both is taken more seriously than one who simply complies or simply objects.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Ask for your branch's P&L split into controllable and allocated. Many businesses have never presented it that way and can produce it easily. It changes what you are accountable for from a number you cannot influence to one you can.

checks.q: Your branch shows a loss after head office allocation. Before accepting that it is failing you should establish:
opts: Its contribution — sales less cost of sales less costs that would genuinely stop
checks.why: An allocated cost does not disappear if the branch does; it redistributes onto the ones that remain.

checks.q: You are asked to find savings at your branch. The line worth looking at first is:
checks.why: It is also the one a manager adjusts weekly, usually from availability and habit rather than from trade.

checks.q: Comparing your staffing profile to your hourly sales profile usually reveals:
opts: Overstaffing in the morning and shortage when trade converts
checks.why: Fixing it costs nothing and improves the cost line and the conversion line at once.

lessons.title: The numbers that lie
lessons.html:
Every branch report contains figures that look precise and are not. Knowing which is not cynicism — it is what stops you defending a number you cannot support, or acting on one that was never real.

Stock valuation. True only as at the last count, and drifting from that moment. If your last count was in March, the September figure is an estimate with a March anchor. Ask when the count was before treating it as fact.

Anything with an allocation in it. Branch profit after head office costs is arithmetic performed on a rule. Change the rule and your branch's profitability changes without a single thing happening in the store.

Like-for-like comparisons across a change. A refit, a range change, a new competitor, a road closure — the comparison is between two different situations. Say so at the time rather than being asked later.

Averages that hide their shape. An average basket of ₦4,200 might be a tight cluster or two entirely different customer groups. Averages across branches are worse — the estate average describes no branch that exists.

Percentages on small numbers. Complaints up 200% means two became six. In a branch of your size most weekly percentages are noise, and reacting to them is how a team gets whiplashed by numbers that meant nothing.

Anything typed rather than derived. The finance and control tracks both make this point and it applies to your own reports: a figure somebody entered into a spreadsheet has been through a human, and humans round, transpose and remember. Ask where a surprising number came from before you act on it.

And the one closest to home: figures you produced yourself. A count you rushed, an availability check done from memory, a footfall estimate. You will trust these more than they deserve precisely because you produced them. Note how each was arrived at, and be as sceptical of your own numbers as of anybody else's.

What to do with all of this. Not distrust everything — use each figure for what it can carry. Stock valuation for direction rather than precision. Contribution rather than allocated profit for whether the branch works. Like-for-like only across comparable periods. And any surprising number checked once before it becomes a decision.

WATCH-OUT: The most dangerous figure on any report is the one you are measured on, because you have the strongest reason to accept it when it is good and to argue with it when it is not. Apply the same scepticism in both directions or you are not being sceptical at all.

How to disagree with a number properly. Not by disputing it in a meeting from memory. Establish what it was built from, find the specific step you think is wrong, and put that in writing with the alternative figure and how you arrived at it. A manager who says a number feels wrong is dismissed; one who says the valuation is anchored on a March count and here is what a current count shows is not. The difference is entirely in the preparation.

checks.q: Your stock valuation shows September and the last count was in March. The figure is:
opts: An estimate anchored on March and drifting since
Only wrong if shrinkage is high
checks.why: Ask when the count was before treating a valuation as fact.

checks.q: Complaints at your branch are up 200% this week. This most likely means:
opts: Two became six, and it is noise
checks.why: Reacting to weekly percentages on small numbers is how a team gets whiplashed by figures that meant nothing.

checks.q: The most dangerous figure on any report is:
opts: The one you are measured on
checks.why: You have the strongest reason to accept it when good and argue when bad — scepticism must run both ways.

lessons.title: Okelewo: what the Ikeja two points cost
lessons.html:
Module 1 left the Ikeja manager with sales up nine per cent and margin down two points, unaware because he read the sales report and not the margin one. This is what it cost and how it was found.

The arithmetic. Ikeja turns over about ₦21,000,000 a month. Two points of margin is ₦420,000 monthly. Over the three quarters it ran, roughly ₦3.8m — against a nine per cent sales increase that added, at the branch's actual margin, about ₦1.4m of gross profit over the same period.

So the branch worked harder, sold more, and earned ₦2.4m less. Every daily report during those three quarters was green.

What caused it, in the order it was found. Decomposition first, not accusation. The category split showed the whole movement sitting in two categories, both of which had been promoted repeatedly. The markdown report — available because the counters record a reason on the line, as the ZhiftPOS track describes — showed the promotional discount running at nearly double its budgeted percentage. And a third of the promotional volume was on lines the branch would have sold anyway.

The manager had not done anything forbidden. He ran promotions he was permitted to run, to hit a sales target he was measured on, and the system recorded every one of them correctly. Nobody was reading the record.

How it surfaced. Not from a report. The finance lead was preparing a group margin analysis, noticed one branch moving against the estate, and asked. That is luck rather than control — and the uncomfortable question afterwards was how long it would have run had she been looking at something else that week.

What changed. The monthly branch call added margin, shrinkage, availability and staff turnover to what had been a sales conversation. Within two quarters Ikeja's manager was reading his margin report, because it had become something he was asked about — the attention lever from module 1, applied downward.

And the point for you. He was not a poor manager. He was a manager reading the report he was given, measured on the number he was shown, doing exactly what that arrangement rewarded. The defence is knowing which numbers you are not being shown, which is the whole of this module.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: If your monthly conversation with your manager covers only sales, you are in the Ikeja position whether or not anything is currently wrong. Bring margin to it yourself, before anybody asks, and the conversation changes permanently.

The wider lesson from Ikeja, which applies well beyond promotions. A person measured on one number will optimise that number, and will do it honestly and energetically. That is not a character flaw and it cannot be trained away — it is what measurement does. So the useful question about any target you are given is what it would cost the business if you hit it by the easiest available route, and whether anybody is watching that cost. If the answer is nobody, say so before you start rather than after three quarters.

checks.q: Ikeja's nine per cent sales rise added ₦1.4m of gross profit while two margin points cost ₦3.8m. The branch:
opts: Worked harder, sold more, and earned ₦2.4m less
checks.why: Every daily report during those three quarters was green.

checks.q: The margin problem was found because:
opts: The finance lead happened to notice one branch moving against the estate
checks.why: That is luck rather than control, and the uncomfortable question is how long it would otherwise have run.

checks.q: If your monthly conversation with your manager covers only sales, you are:
opts: In the Ikeja position, whether or not anything is currently wrong
checks.why: Bring margin to it yourself, before anybody asks.

lessons.title: The manager's weekly numbers
lessons.html:
This is the chapter to keep. Six figures, weekly, in about fifteen minutes — and the discipline is that they are the same six every week, because a number is only useful once you know what normal looks like.

1. Transactions and basket, against the same week last year. Two numbers, and between them they explain almost any sales movement. Not against last week — against the comparable week.

2. Margin percentage, against the prior month. The number your sales report will not tell you and the one that quietly costs the most. If you can only add one figure to what you currently see, add this.

3. Availability on your top forty by contribution. Counted, not estimated. Fifteen minutes twice a week, and it is the largest recoverable loss you have.

4. Markdown value and its top reason. Not just how much was given away but why, which the counter records if it is configured as it should be.

5. Hours against trade. Whether the rota matched the shape of the week, which is both the largest controllable cost and a conversion lever.

6. One thing from the floor. Not a number. Something you saw — a queue that did not move, a category customers kept asking about, a member of staff who has gone quiet. The figures tell you what happened; this tells you what is about to.

Why the same six. A number in isolation means nothing. Twelve weeks of the same six means you know your branch's normal, and you notice a departure in the week it starts rather than in the quarter it shows up. That is the entire value, and it comes from consistency rather than sophistication.

Write them down and keep them. Most managers look and move on. A retained series turns a snapshot into a trend, and a trend is the difference between noticing that something is unusual and noticing that something has changed — only the second is worth acting on.

And what to do with the six. One of them will be moving in a direction you do not like. That one becomes the cause you spend module 1's protected hour on. Not all six, and not whichever is loudest — the one that is both moving and worth money.

IMPLEMENTATION TIP: Put the six on one sheet, same day each week, and keep twelve weeks of them where you can see the series at once. Fifteen minutes weekly is three hours a quarter, and it is the difference between managing your branch and being informed about it afterwards.

What to do when the six all look fine. Most weeks they will, and that is the point — a routine whose value only appears when something is wrong still has to be run on the weeks nothing is. Record the quiet week and move on. The value is not in what any single week tells you; it is that the twelfth week tells you something the first eleven made visible, and there is no way to get the twelfth without the eleven.

checks.q: If you could add only one figure to a standard sales report, it should be:
checks.why: It is the number the sales report will not tell you and the one that quietly costs the most.

checks.q: The sixth weekly item is one thing from the floor rather than a number because:
opts: The figures tell you what happened; the floor tells you what is about to
checks.why: A queue that did not move, a category customers kept asking about, a member of staff gone quiet.

checks.q: The value of tracking the same six figures weekly comes from:
opts: Consistency — twelve weeks tells you what normal looks like
checks.why: You notice a departure in the week it starts rather than the quarter it shows up.

questions.q: A standard branch reporting pack is missing margin, availability, isolated shrinkage and:
questions.why: It usually mixes costs you decide with costs allocated from the centre.

questions.q: Before reading any report you should ask who produced it and:
questions.why: A figure from the system is different evidence from one typed into a spreadsheet.

questions.q: A request for a figure you do not currently receive works best when it:
opts: Names the figure and the reason you need it
questions.why: The data usually exists and nobody asked for it in that shape.

questions.q: If the answer to a reporting request is no, the useful response is to:
opts: Build the two or three numbers roughly yourself
questions.why: Three months of hand-tracking is a much stronger case for it being reported properly.

questions.q: Sales equals transactions multiplied by:
questions.why: And transactions are footfall multiplied by conversion — four numbers under the one.

questions.q: Which part of the sales equation is least within a branch manager's control?
questions.why: Worth knowing precisely so you can say what happened without sounding defensive.

questions.q: A conversion drop with footfall steady is:
questions.why: The single most useful signal on the list.

questions.q: Where footfall is not measured, the usable substitute is:
questions.why: Against last year at the same point in the week.

questions.q: A missed target can mean the branch underperformed or:
questions.why: A manager who can distinguish the two with four numbers is worth listening to.

questions.q: The four movers of margin, in the order a branch manager should check them:
questions.why: Buying price last, because you can rarely act on it and it is what most managers reach for first.

questions.q: Mix is missed most often because:
opts: Every individual product margin still looks correct
questions.why: A month heavy in low-margin categories drops blended margin with nothing wrong anywhere.

questions.q: Two points of margin on ₦18m monthly turnover is worth annually about:
questions.why: Usually larger than every cost saving a branch manager is asked to find.

questions.q: On noticing a margin fall you should first:
opts: Decompose it by category, markdown reason and cost
questions.why: A specific finding gets acted on where a general concern gets nodded at.

questions.q: Availability should be measured on your top lines ranked by:
questions.why: The biggest sellers are not always where the money is.

questions.q: A system report of lines at zero will not tell you:
opts: How long it was out or how often
questions.why: Which is why a manual count twice a week is worth keeping.

questions.q: A line selling four a day at ₦1,200 with 30% margin, out for nine days, costs roughly:
questions.why: Converting availability to money is what gets a replenishment problem taken seriously.

questions.q: Which cause of unavailability is invisible to every count you will do?
questions.why: It is a layout problem rather than a stock one.

questions.q: The most frequent cause of a gap is:
opts: Delivered but not on the shelf
questions.why: A branch losing sales on goods it has already paid for.

questions.q: The largest component of shrinkage is usually:
questions.why: Miscounts, mis-scans, wrong units and cut-off mistakes.

questions.q: Treating all shrinkage as theft causes a manager to:
opts: Spend attention on the smallest component
questions.why: And on the part involving their own staff, which is corrosive and usually wrong.

questions.q: Shrinkage should be compared:
questions.why: Naira ranks by branch size and tells you nothing.

questions.q: A receiver whose quantities always match the order exactly is:
questions.why: Real deliveries are occasionally short, damaged or over.

questions.q: A count performed by whoever is responsible for the stock is:
questions.why: Rotating who counts what costs nothing and changes the quality of the number.

questions.q: The largest controllable cost in most branches is:
questions.why: And the one a manager adjusts weekly.

questions.q: A branch showing a loss after allocation may still be:
questions.why: Closing it would redistribute the overhead onto the branches that remain.

questions.q: The figure that says whether your branch earns its keep is:
questions.why: Sales less cost of sales less the costs that would genuinely stop.

questions.q: Comparing staffing profile to hourly sales profile typically shows:
opts: Overstaffing in the morning and shortage when trade converts
questions.why: Fixing it costs nothing and improves cost and conversion together.

questions.q: Cost reduction at branch level is:
opts: Real and small, usually smaller than margin or availability
questions.why: Which is why the earlier chapters come first in this module.

questions.q: A stock valuation is true only:
questions.why: Ask when the count was before treating it as fact.

questions.q: Branch profit after head office costs is:
opts: Arithmetic performed on a rule somebody chose
questions.why: Change the rule and your branch's profitability changes with nothing happening in the store.

questions.q: An estate average describes:
questions.why: Averages across branches hide their shape entirely.

questions.q: Complaints up 200% in a branch of your size is usually:
questions.why: Two became six.

questions.q: Figures you produced yourself deserve:
opts: The same scepticism as anybody else's
questions.why: You will trust them more than they deserve precisely because you produced them.

questions.q: Ikeja turned over ₦21m monthly. Two points of margin cost:
questions.why: Roughly ₦3.8m across the three quarters it ran.

questions.q: The nine per cent sales rise added ₦1.4m of gross profit, so the branch was:
questions.why: Every daily report during those three quarters was green.

questions.q: The Ikeja problem was found by:
opts: The finance lead noticing one branch moving against the estate
questions.why: Luck rather than control.

questions.q: The Ikeja manager had:
opts: Done exactly what the arrangement rewarded
questions.why: He ran permitted promotions to hit the number he was measured on, and the system recorded every one.

questions.q: What changed afterwards was that the monthly branch call added margin, shrinkage, availability and:
questions.why: The attention lever from module 1, applied downward.

questions.q: How many figures are in the weekly routine?
questions.why: About fifteen minutes, the same six every week.

questions.q: Transactions and basket should be compared against:
questions.why: Not against last week — against the comparable week.

questions.q: The sixth weekly item is:
opts: One thing from the floor, not a number
questions.why: The figures tell you what happened; this tells you what is about to.

questions.q: The value of the weekly six comes from:
opts: Consistency, so you learn what normal looks like
questions.why: Twelve weeks of the same six means you notice a departure in the week it starts.

questions.q: Which of the six should become your protected hour's work?
opts: The one both moving and worth money
questions.why: Not all six, and not whichever is loudest.
